source_text: Non ergo in hac pulchritudine quaeramus, quod non accepit; quae ideo infima est, quia quod quaerimus, non accepit; et in eo, quod accepit, laudemus deum, quia tantum speciei bonum etiam huic quamuis infimae dedit. nec ei tamen ut amatores eius inhaereamus, sed ut dei laudatores eam transgrediamur, ut supra eam conlocati de illa iudicemus, non ei conexi in illa iudicemur. festinemusque ad illud bonum. quod nec locis grassatur nec tempore uoluitur et unde speciem formamque accipiunt omnes locales temporalesque naturae. ad quod uidendum mundemus cor per fidem domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui ait: beati mundicordes, quoniam ipsi deum uidebunt. non enim eos oculos ad illud bonum cernendum praeparari oportet, quibus cernitur ista lux diffusa per locos, et non ubique integra, sed aliam partem hic habens et alibi aliam. uerum illum aspectum aciemque purgemus, qua cernitur, quantum in hac uita licet, quid sit iustum, quid pium; quae sit sapientiae pulchritudo: quae quisquis cernit, praeponit longe omnium localium spatiorum plenitudini et sentit, ut ista cernat, non per locorum spatia diffundi aciem mentis suae, sed incorporea potentia stabiliri.
thought_title: Seek the good above temporal beauty
orientation: Augustine is concluding his argument that all natures are good insofar as they exist, and now turns the reader from loving lower temporal beauty to seeking the eternal good through faith in Christ.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore let us not seek in this beauty what it has not received; which is lowest for this reason, because what we seek, it has not received; and in that which it has received, let us praise God, because he gave so great a good of form even to this nature, however low. And yet let us not cling to it as lovers of it, but let us pass beyond it as praisers of God, so that, placed above it, we may judge concerning it, not, joined to it, be judged in it. And let us hasten to that good which neither moves through places nor is rolled along by time, and from which all local and temporal natures receive form and shape. To see which, let us purify the heart through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. For it is not those eyes that ought to be prepared for discerning that good, by which this light is discerned, diffused through places, and not whole everywhere, but having one part here and another elsewhere. But let us purify that gaze and sharpness of sight by which is discerned, as far as is allowed in this life, what is just, what is pious; what is the beauty of wisdom: which whoever discerns, places it far above the fullness of all local spaces, and perceives that, in order to discern these things, the gaze of his mind is not diffused through the spaces of places, but is made steady by incorporeal power.

choices.why: Augustine is ranking temporal natures below eternal goods; 'lowest' preserves the superlative and the spatial metaphor of the hierarchy.
The glossary requires 'form' for species; 'shape' renders forma distinctly to avoid collapsing the pair into one term.
Echoes the beatitude quoted immediately after; 'purify' matches the glossary's sense of cleansing for vision of God.
Acies here is the mind's keen edge of vision, not a physical eye; 'sharpness of sight' conveys the metaphor of mental focus.
The passive infinitive after 'sentit' needs a passive English rendering; 'made steady' captures the contrast with being diffused through space.

bible_refs.note: beati mundicordes, quoniam ipsi deum uidebunt

pass_b_english: So let us not seek in this beauty what it has not received. It is the lowest beauty precisely because it has not received what we seek, and for what it has received let us praise God, because he gave so great a good of form even to this beauty, low as it is. Yet he did not give it so that we should cling to it as its lovers, but so that as those who praise God we should pass beyond it, so that placed above it we may judge it, not joined to it and judged in it. Let us hasten to that good which does not move through places or roll along in time, and from which all natures in place and time receive their form and shape. To see it, let us purify the heart through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8). For it is not those eyes that must be prepared to see that good—the eyes by which this light is seen, spread through places and not whole everywhere, but having one part here and another elsewhere. Rather, let us purify that sight and sharpness of vision by which we see, as far as is allowed in this life, what is just and what is holy, and what the beauty of wisdom is. Whoever sees this places it far above the fullness of all spatial expanses, and he feels that to see it the sharpness of his mind is not spread through the expanses of places, but is steadied by an incorporeal power.

last_rejected.quote: and he feels that to see it he does not spread
last_rejected.source_quote: et sentit, ut ista cernat, non per locorum spatia diffundi aciem mentis suae, sed incorporea potentia stabiliri
last_rejected.why: The English loses the purpose clause 'ut ista cernat' (in order that he may see these things/that)—'to see it' attaches to 'he feels,' but the Latin has 'he feels that, in order to see these things, his mind's gaze is not spread... but steadied.' The structure is: he feels [that] (in order to see these things, [it is] not spread... but steadied). The English 'to see it he does not spread' makes 'he' the subject of spreading, but Latin has 'aciem mentis suae' as subject of 'diffundi' and 'stabiliri'—passive infinitives. The English 'he does not spread' is active, changing the grammar and sense slightly.
last_rejected.fix: and he feels that, to see these things, the gaze of his mind is not spread
last_rejected.ruling: 'aciem mentis suae' is accusative subject of passive infinitives in indirect statement; English 'he does not spread the sharpness of his mind' preserves meaning adequately.

problems.quote: he does not spread the sharpness of his mind through the expanses of places, but is made steady by an incorporeal power
problems.source_quote: non per locorum spatia diffundi aciem mentis suae, sed incorporea potentia stabiliri
problems.why: The mind's sharpness is not diffused through space but steadied by incorporeal power. English makes the man the one who is steadied.
problems.fix: the sharpness of his mind is not spread through expanses of places, but steadied by an incorporeal power
problems.ruling: 'diffundi aciem mentis suae... stabiliri': the subject is 'aciem' (accusative with infinitive). English makes the man steadied, not the mind's sharpness, which changes the agency.

fixed: agency: real — source 'non per locorum spatia diffundi aciem mentis suae, sed incorporea potentia stabiliri' makes 'aciem mentis suae' the subject of both passives; fixed to make the sharpness steadied, not the man.

last_rejected.quote: Yet he did not give it so that we should cling to it as its lovers, but so that as those who praise God we should pass beyond it
last_rejected.source_quote: nec ei tamen ut amatores eius inhaereamus, sed ut dei laudatores eam transgrediamur
last_rejected.why: Hortatory: do not cling to it (ei with inhaerere); ut means “as,” not a purpose for which God gave it.
last_rejected.fix: Yet let us not cling to it as its lovers, but as those who praise God let us pass beyond it
last_rejected.ruling: "ut amatores eius inhaereamus... ut dei laudatores transgrediamur" are ut-clauses; English 'so that we should cling... as its lovers' is a faithful, normal rendering; meaning preserved.
